site.name: meadowos
site.summary: meadowos-clone Fictional self-hosted home OS "MeadowOS" marketing site (magazine / zine-style long-scroll narrative). Pages | File | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `index.html` | Single-page long scroll: thin top nav + progress bar; hero with hand-drawn SVG house and flower illustration; five chapters (Roman numerals I–V) of magazine-prose with pull quotes and chapter illustrations; mid-page "Garden" 6-card plant-app grid (Nextfile / Bramble / Cottage / Smithy / Hearth / Postcard); reviewer quotes; terminal-style .iso download block + platform pills + minimum / recommended specs; six numbered manifesto items; dark footer | | `styles.css` | Brand color #2F5233 dark green, accent terracotta + wheat yellow, cream paper background; Crimson Pro serif + Inter; cards with slight rotate + paper-shadow; responsive | | `script.js` | Top scroll progress bar; smooth anchor scrolling; clicking "Download .iso" triggers a fake download-progress modal (increments to 100% then shows SHA256 verification passed) |

explored_user_goal: Autonomously explore and critique the UX of the full meadowos system, prioritizing the primary landing flow plus adjacent pages, states, and recovery paths.
exploration_summary: The MeadowOS landing page offers a visually appealing, magazine-style long-scroll experience with highly readable typography, responsive layouts, and a clever top reading progress bar. However, the UX is significantly hindered by accessibility gaps, particularly missing keyboard focus states. Furthermore, mobile users suffer from the complete removal of section navigation links, forcing tedious manual scrolling.

exploration_plan.goal: Exhaustively explore and critique the single-page MeadowOS marketing site, focusing on navigation, scroll behaviors, interactive modal states, and mobile responsiveness.
exploration_plan.summary: The exploration will validate the long-scroll narrative structure of MeadowOS. It will start by testing the top navigation anchor links and scroll progress bar on desktop. Then it will trigger and validate the fake download modal's progression and completion states. Finally, it will evaluate the mobile viewport, paying special attention to the layout of the 'Garden' grid and previously identified small tap targets.
assumptions: The site is a single page (index.html) with internal anchor links.
Clicking the download button triggers a simulated modal rather than an actual file download.
The scroll progress bar updates dynamically as the user scrolls down.
risk_hotspots: Small tap targets in the top navigation and footer links
Fake download modal state transitions (progress to SHA256 verification)
Layout of the 'Garden' 6-card plant-app grid on mobile

phases.title: Navigation and Scrolling
phases.objective: Verify that top navigation links smoothly scroll to their respective sections and the scroll progress bar updates.
key_checks: Click 'Story', 'Garden', 'Docs', and 'Get the .iso' and verify the viewport scrolls to the correct anchors
Observe if a scroll progress bar is visible and updates its width/state based on scroll depth
exit_criteria: All top navigation links have been clicked and their target sections verified.

phases.title: Download Modal Interaction
phases.objective: Test the fake '.iso' download flow and its state changes.
key_checks: Verify a modal appears showing download progress
Wait and verify the progress reaches 100% and displays the SHA256 verification success message
exit_criteria: The download modal has been triggered, fully completed its simulated process, and closed.

phases.title: Mobile Viewport and Layout Validation
phases.objective: Check responsive layout, specifically the 'Garden' grid, narrative text readability, and tap target sizes.
key_checks: Examine the top navigation (check if it collapses or remains thin, verify tap target usability)
Scroll down to the 'Garden' section and ensure the 6-card grid stacks or adjusts appropriately without overflow
Check footer links (GitHub, Matrix room) for accessibility/tap target size
exit_criteria: Mobile layout has been fully scrolled and visually inspected for overflows or usability issues.

coverage_targets.pages: Fully scroll and explore index.html on both desktop and mobile.
coverage_targets.features: Test all anchor links, the fake download modal flow, and hover/active states.
coverage_targets.mobile: Validate mobile layout for the 6-card grid and assess small tap targets identified in prescan.

notes: Pay attention to the typography and 'zine-style' layout elements to ensure they do not break across different screen widths.

findings.user_goal: Quickly jump to specific sections of interest, such as the app grid or download area, on a mobile device.
findings.problem: The sticky top navigation on mobile removes the main section links ('Story', 'Garden', 'Docs', 'Get the .iso'), leaving only the logo and read time.
findings.evidence: Trajectory chunk steps-43-48 reports: 'The sticky top navigation on mobile removes the right-side links... leaving only the logo and read time, which prevents crowding but limits navigation options.'
findings.why_it_matters: On a long-scrolling, text-heavy page, removing jump links forces mobile users to manually scroll extensively to find key content, causing high friction and potential drop-off.
findings.suggestion: Implement a collapsed mobile menu (e.g., a hamburger menu) or a horizontally scrollable nav bar to retain access to crucial section links on small screens.
findings.source_hint: Top navigation header component on mobile breakpoints

findings.user_goal: Navigate and interact with the site using a keyboard instead of a mouse.
findings.problem: Sequential tab navigation does not trigger visible focus rings or style changes on the top navigation links or other interactive elements.
findings.evidence: Trajectory chunk steps-25-30 notes: 'Keyboard navigation using the 'Tab' key does not produce a visible focus ring on the top navigation links... indicating a lack of accessible focus states.'
findings.why_it_matters: Users with motor impairments or those who rely on keyboard navigation cannot visually determine which element currently holds focus, making the site practically unusable for them.
findings.suggestion: Add distinct `:focus-visible` CSS rules (e.g., outlines or specific background/text color changes) for all links and buttons to clearly indicate keyboard focus.

findings.user_goal: Understand current position within the narrative structure while freely scrolling.
findings.problem: The top navigation links do not update their active state (highlighting) when the user manually scrolls through the corresponding sections of the page.
findings.evidence: Trajectory chunk steps-25-30 states: 'The navigation links ('Story', 'Garden', 'Docs') do not exhibit a visible active state or highlight as the user scrolls through their corresponding sections'.
findings.why_it_matters: Without dynamic wayfinding cues, users scrolling through a long, single-page site can easily lose context of where they are relative to the overall site structure.
findings.suggestion: Implement an Intersection Observer in JavaScript to detect which section is currently in view and dynamically apply the active squiggly-underline style to the matching navigation link.

findings.user_goal: Tap on footer links to view external community pages.
findings.problem: The 'GitHub' and 'Matrix room' links in the footer have very small tap targets (16px high) on mobile devices.
findings.evidence: The final layout warnings report: 'Tap target is 43x16px' and 'Tap target is 74x16px, below the 44px mobile guidance.'
findings.why_it_matters: Small touch targets make it difficult for users to tap accurately on touchscreens, increasing the likelihood of frustrating accidental clicks on adjacent elements.
findings.suggestion: Increase the padding on the footer anchor tags to ensure they meet the minimum recommended touch target size of 44x44px.

findings.user_goal: Click footer links to view the source code or community chat.
findings.problem: The external footer links are implemented with `href="#"`, which abruptly scrolls the user to the very top of the page when clicked.
findings.evidence: Trajectory chunk steps-07-12 observes: 'The 'GitHub' link in the footer is an empty anchor (href="#"). Clicking it appends a '#' to the URL and scrolls the user to the top of the page'.
findings.why_it_matters: While this is likely a fictional marketing site, unexpectedly losing one's place at the bottom of a long scroll by being thrown to the top is a jarring experience that feels like a bug.
findings.suggestion: Prevent the default top-scroll behavior using JavaScript (`event.preventDefault()`) or use `href="javascript:void(0)"`. Even better, display a 'Coming Soon' tooltip on click.
